Darnell and Darnell: scholarly translation of primary texts with commentary, published in a peer-reviewed academic series (SBL Writings from the Ancient World).

exact_quotes: Note: German quotes from Kockelmann are verbatim except that umlauts and eszett are written without diacritics (o for ö, a for ä, u for ü, ss for ß). Dashes in Darnell quotes replaced as marked.

Kockelmann, WiBiLex s.v. Apophis, section 2: 'Apophis ist in der agyptischen Religion die Verkorperung der Machte des Ungeordneten und des Nichtseins par excellence. Entsprechend hatte Apophis nicht den Status einer Gottheit, er verfugte weder uber einen eigenen Kult noch wurden Statuen von ihm hergestellt.' (Gloss: 'In Egyptian religion Apophis is the embodiment of the powers of disorder and non-being par excellence. Accordingly Apophis did not have the status of a deity; he had no cult of his own and no statues of him were made.')

Kockelmann, section 1: the Greek form renders Egyptian '3pp / 'p'p, 'was moglicherweise mit "Grosser-an-Rumoren" ubersetzt werden kann' (gloss: 'which can possibly be translated as "Great of Rumbling"'); in Coptic the name survives as aphoph / aphopi meaning 'giant' ('Riese').
Kockelmann, section 2: 'Typisch ist seine Gestalt als gewaltige Schlange von 120 Ellen (ca. 62 m) Lange' (gloss: 'Typical is his form as a huge serpent 120 cubits (about 62 m) long').

Kockelmann, section 2: 'Die alteste namentliche Erwahnung des Apophis ist in den Inschriften des Grabes des Anchtifi uberliefert (1. Zwischenzeit, Ende drittes Jahrtausend v. Chr.). Erste konkrete Anspielungen auf den Konflikt zwischen Re und Apophis finden sich in den etwas jungeren Sargtexten.' (Gloss: 'The oldest mention of Apophis by name is preserved in the inscriptions of the tomb of Ankhtifi (First Intermediate Period, end of the third millennium BC). The first concrete allusions to the conflict between Re and Apophis are found in the somewhat later Coffin Texts.')

Kockelmann, section 2: 'Durch das Einschlurfen des Fahrwassers der Sonnenbarke des Re und mit den barriereartigen Windungen seines Schlangenleibes droht er die Fahrt des Gottes zum Stillstand zu bringen. Als Wesen des Chaos gehort er zwar der dunklen Welttiefe an, nahert sich aber wahrend der gesamten Nachtfahrt des Re immer wieder drohend dem Sonnenboot an.' (Gloss: 'By slurping up the channel water of Re's sun barque and with the barrier-like coils of his serpent body he threatens to bring the god's journey to a standstill. As a being of chaos he belongs to the dark depths of the world, but throughout Re's entire night journey he again and again approaches the sun boat threateningly.')

Kockelmann, section 2: 'Hauptquelle fur den taglichen Kampf des Sonnengottes und seiner Barkenmannschaft gegen die Chaosschlange Apophis sind die koniglichen Unterweltsbucher des Neuen Reiches ... (insbesondere "Amduat" und "Pfortenbuch")' (gloss: 'The main source for the daily battle of the sun god and his barque crew against the chaos serpent Apophis is the royal netherworld books of the New Kingdom ... (especially the Amduat and the Book of Gates)').

Kockelmann, section 2: 'Prominenter Bekampfer des Apophis und Helfer des Re ist der Gott Seth. Er wird haufig am Bug der Sonnenbarke gezeigt, von wo aus er die Apophisschlange mit seinem Speer durchbohrt ... Nach Totenbuch-Spruch 108 bewirkt er durch den Stoss mit der Lanze, dass der Sonnenfeind das bereits verschluckte Fahrwasser wieder ausspeit, so dass die Fahrt fortgesetzt werden kann.' (Gloss: 'A prominent fighter against Apophis and helper of Re is the god Seth. He is often shown at the prow of the sun barque, from where he pierces the Apophis serpent with his spear ... According to Book of the Dead spell 108, his lance thrust makes the sun's enemy spit out the channel water he has already swallowed, so the journey can continue.')

Kockelmann, section 2: 'Wahrend der Spatzeit wird Seth als Morder des Osiris in weiten Teilen des Landes allerdings selbst zum Inbegriff des "Gotterfeindes" und ahnlich vehement bekampft wie Apophis.' (Gloss: 'In the Late Period, however, Seth as murderer of Osiris himself becomes in large parts of the country the epitome of the "enemy of the gods" and is fought almost as vehemently as Apophis.')

Kockelmann, section 2: 'Als Zeichen der Verfemung wird sein Name in den agyptischen Papyri oft rot geschrieben. Die rituelle Vernichtung des Sonnenfeindes unter allen seinen Bezeichnungen wird im sogenannten "Apophisbuch" geschildert, das vollstandig auf einem Papyrus des spaten 4. Jh.s v. Chr. uberliefert ist.' (Gloss: 'As a sign of proscription his name is often written in red in Egyptian papyri. The ritual annihilation of the sun's enemy under all his names is described in the so-called Book of Apophis, preserved complete on a papyrus of the late 4th century BC.')
Darnell and Darnell, p. 11: 'the combat against the giant serpent Apep whose defeat and destruction appear textually and/or pictorially in all of the compositions that form a part of the corpus.'

Darnell and Darnell, p. 11: 'Geographically, the defeat of Apep can appear in the middle of the night as well as at sunrise; thus the solar god's combat against the serpent is an ongoing process throughout the nightly journey rather than a single event.'

Darnell and Darnell, p. 11: 'In Hour 7 of the Book of the Hidden Chamber, Isis and the Elder Magician enchant Apep with their spells, while a goddess, She Who Makes Throats Breathe, lassoes the creature, and other deities stab knives deep into his flesh (Regen 2015).'

Darnell and Darnell, p. 11 n. 24: 'For the earlier history of Apep, see Morenz 2004 and references therein (particularly to the inscriptions of Ankhtyfy at Moalla). Ptolemaic texts give Apep a length of 120 cubits (Borghouts 2007, 9 n. 4).'
Darnell and Darnell, p. 11 n. 25: 'The combat against Apep continues during the hours of the day, as represented in the Book of the Day (Muller-Roth 2008, 471-81).'

Darnell and Darnell, p. 11 n. 26: 'The Elder Magician (hkA smsw) is not a hypostasis of Seth (Hornung 1963b, 131), but rather Heka as the eldest son of the creator deity (te Velde 1969-1970; Ritner 1993, 18-20).'

Darnell and Darnell, p. 12, Book of Gates Hour 10 Scene 66 incantation: 'Hail, rebel, away, Apep, one to whom his evil is given. May your face be destroyed, O Apep, make a way to the slaughtering place. Knives be against you, you having already been cut; the Old Ones be against you, you having already been destroyed ... Hail, the destroyed one is driven back, the Fettered Serpent is annihilated' (p. 313). [Dashes in the printed translation replaced with commas here.]

Darnell and Darnell, p. 12: 'In the following Scene 67, Apep is again destroyed so that the solar bark can sail past successfully ... Apep must be annihilated again in the final hour of the night, in order to ensure the successful rising of the sun in the eastern horizon (Scene 89).'

Darnell and Darnell, pp. 12-13: in the tomb of Ramesses VI 'the scarab Khepri emerges from the "coils" of Apep, suggesting that the chaos serpent, like the waters of Nun, can provide a regenerative force for the solar god.'

Darnell and Darnell, p. 135 (Amduat overview): 'Hour 7 juxtaposes the destruction of Re's ultimate enemy, Apep, with the ordering of time ... The evil serpent is defeated by physical means (binding and slicing) as well as through magical spells spoken by Isis and the Elder Magician (see p. 196). The defeat of Apep allows time itself to proceed, and Horus orders the hours in Register 3.' [Parenthesis replaces printed dashes.]

Darnell and Darnell, p. 199, Amduat Hour 7 Register 1 text: 'These spells of Isis and the Elder Magician are performed for the repelling of Apep from Re, in the West, in the hidden part of the Netherworld. This is done on earth likewise.'

Darnell and Darnell, p. 200, Amduat Hour 7 Scene 75, label to Apep: 'Bringer of Water is the name of this sandbank; (it is) 440 cubits in its length and 440 cubits in its width. It is his voice that leads the gods against him. He always moves when this great god passes by this locale.'

Darnell and Darnell, p. 200, label to the punishing goddesses: 'It is these goddesses who punish Apep in the Netherworld, who repel the actions of the enemies of Re. They exist in this fashion bearing their knives, so that they might punish Apep in the Netherworld daily.'
Darnell and Darnell, p. 200: 'One who knows it on earth is one whose water Terrible of Face will not drink.'

Darnell and Darnell, p. 329, Book of Gates Hour 12 Scene 89 description: 'Nine gods ... "The Ennead that Punishes Apep" brandish scepters and knives. The object of their aggression is a serpent, "Apep," who is tied to stakes labeled the "Children of Horus."'
date_and_recency: Morenz 2004 (July 2004 issue). Kockelmann entry created January 2009, revised versions dated 2017 and 2018. Darnell and Darnell 2018. Material discussed: first named attestation of Apophis in the tomb of Ankhtifi at Moalla, First Intermediate Period (Kockelmann: end of the third millennium BC; Morenz per secondary report: 9th Dynasty) [uncertain for the Morenz dynasty attribution]; Coffin Texts (Middle Kingdom); royal netherworld books (Amduat, Book of Gates) of the New Kingdom; Book of Apophis on a papyrus of the late 4th century BC; Ptolemaic temple texts (Esna; the 120-cubit length).
key_claims: Kockelmann: Apophis embodies disorder and non-being par excellence; he did not have the status of a deity, had no cult and no statues.
Kockelmann: the name is the Greek form of Egyptian '3pp, possibly 'Great of Rumbling'; Coptic aphoph means 'giant'.

Kockelmann: usual form a huge serpent of 120 cubits; alternatively a turtle; many aliases (Swallower, 'the evil one', etc.); an Esna text has Apophis born from Re's umbilical cord, and Plutarch calls him the sun god's brother.

Kockelmann: oldest named mention in the tomb of Ankhtifi (First Intermediate Period); first concrete allusions to the Re-Apophis conflict in the Coffin Texts, where he is driven off by magic and bound.
Kockelmann: Apophis tries to halt the solar cycle by drinking the barque's channel water and blocking it with his coils; he threatens the boat again and again throughout the night journey.
Kockelmann: the main source for the daily battle is the New Kingdom royal netherworld books, especially the Amduat and Book of Gates.

Kockelmann: Seth is a prominent defender of Re, spearing Apophis from the prow; in BD 108 his spear makes Apophis spit out the swallowed water. In the Late Period Seth himself is demonised as the 'enemy of the gods'.

Kockelmann: Apophis's many aliases describe him as already destroyed ('the cut-up one', 'the punished one'); his name is often written in red; his ritual annihilation is set out in the Book of Apophis (late 4th century BC papyrus).

Darnell and Darnell: Apep's defeat and destruction appear in every composition of the netherworld book corpus; the combat is 'an ongoing process throughout the nightly journey rather than a single event', and it continues through the hours of the day (Book of the Day).

Darnell and Darnell: in Amduat Hour 7, Isis and the Elder Magician enchant Apep while She Who Makes Throats Breathe lassoes him and Chief of His Knives stabs him; the knife goddesses punish Apep 'daily'. The Elder Magician is Heka, not Seth.
Darnell and Darnell: in the Book of Gates Apep is destroyed repeatedly (Hours 3, 6, 10 Scenes 66, 67, 69) and must be 'annihilated again' in Hour 12 (Scene 89) for the sun to rise.
Darnell and Darnell: in Ramesses VI's tomb Khepri emerges from Apep's coils, hinting that the serpent, like Nun, can also feed solar regeneration.
Morenz 2004 (not read; via citations): Apophis as an 'anti-god' and 'enemy of order'; discusses origin and name, with the Ankhtifi inscriptions as the earliest attestation [uncertain].
headline_figures: 120 cubits: Apophis's length, Kockelmann ('120 Ellen (ca. 62 m)'); Darnell and Darnell p. 11 n. 24 attribute the figure to Ptolemaic texts (citing Borghouts 2007, 9 n. 4).
440 cubits: length and width of Apep's sandbank 'Bringer of Water' in Amduat Hour 7 Scene 75 (Darnell and Darnell p. 200: '440 cubits in its length and 440 cubits in its width').
Hour 7 of 12: the hour of the Amduat in which Apep is overcome (Darnell and Darnell pp. 135, 196-200).
Hour 12, Scene 89: Book of Gates, nine gods ('The Ennead that Punishes Apep') and the four Children of Horus as stakes (Darnell and Darnell p. 329).
13 deities with throw-nets in Book of Gates Hour 10 Scene 66 (Darnell and Darnell p. 12: 'thirteen throw-net wielding deities').
End of the third millennium BC: date of the first named mention (tomb of Ankhtifi, First Intermediate Period), Kockelmann.
Late 4th century BC: date of the papyrus that preserves the complete Book of Apophis (Kockelmann; i.e. Papyrus Bremner-Rhind).
JNES 63(3), pp. 201-205: Morenz 2004, a five-page article.
dating_and_context: Not an excavation report. First attestation: inscriptions of the tomb of the nomarch Ankhtifi at Moalla (Mo'alla), First Intermediate Period, end of the third millennium BC (Kockelmann; Darnell and Darnell n. 24 point to Morenz 2004 for the Ankhtifi references). The Re-Apophis combat appears first in the Coffin Texts (Middle Kingdom), is laid out in detail in the New Kingdom royal tomb books (Amduat, Book of Gates, versions in tombs of Thutmose III, Seti I, Ramesses VI and others), and the full ritual book survives on a late 4th-century BC papyrus. Darnell and Darnell translate from the New Kingdom royal tomb versions with variants from later sarcophagi.
what_it_says_about_apophis: Apophis (Apep) is the giant chaos serpent, the embodiment of disorder and non-being, and not a god: no cult, no statues (Kockelmann; Morenz's 'anti-god' label points the same way). Every night he tries to stop the sun barque by drinking its water and blocking it with his coils, and he comes back again and again across the night. Defenders: Seth spearing from the prow (BD 108, New Kingdom iconography), and in the Amduat Hour 7 Isis and the Elder Magician (Heka), who disable him with spells while other deities lasso, bind and stab him; in the Book of Gates the Ennead, the Children of Horus and goddesses with nets and knives. Is he ever finally destroyed? No. He is 'destroyed' in scene after scene and his very names call him already cut up, yet he must be 'annihilated again' in the last hour, the knife goddesses punish him 'daily', and the fight carries on through the day hours. Darnell and Darnell state it plainly: 'an ongoing process ... rather than a single event'. No source read here describes a final, permanent end to Apophis.
ritual_practice: Neither source is a ritual manual, but both point to practice on earth. Amduat Hour 7 says the spells of Isis and the Elder Magician against Apep are 'done on earth likewise', and that one who knows the image 'on earth' is one whose water Terrible of Face will not drink (Darnell and Darnell pp. 199-200). Kockelmann notes Apophis's name is often written in red in papyri as a mark of proscription, and that the ritual destruction of the sun's enemy under all his names is set out in the Book of Apophis (late 4th century BC papyrus). The mythic methods (spells, lassoing, binding, knives, spears) mirror the ritual acts of the Bremner-Rhind manual, but the who and where of performance are not covered by these sources.
prescribed_vs_attested_frequency: Within the myth the combat is nightly and repeated: Kockelmann's 'taglichen Kampf' (daily battle), Darnell and Darnell's punishment of Apep 'daily' (Amduat Hour 7 label) and repeated destruction across several hours of each night, plus the day hours. That is a mythic frequency, not evidence of how often priests performed a ritual. These sources say nothing about attested ritual frequency.
relevance_to_angle: Strong support. The scholarly reading matches the essay's angle: chaos is pushed back every night by a crew working together (Isis, Heka, Seth, lasso and knife deities, the Ennead, the Children of Horus), not killed once by a lone hero. Darnell and Darnell's 'ongoing process ... rather than a single event' is a quotable scholarly statement of this. Complications: (1) the texts repeatedly say Apep is 'destroyed' and 'annihilated', so the myth narrates victory each time, just a victory that does not last; (2) Re's own spells and Seth's spear give some heroic individual focus, so 'no single hero' needs care; (3) the Ramesses VI scene where Khepri emerges from Apep's coils suggests chaos is also part of renewal, not purely an enemy, which nuances a simple order-versus-chaos framing; (4) Seth, a defender in the New Kingdom, is himself demonised in the Late Period, so who counts as a maintainer shifts over time.
limitations_stated: Kockelmann hedges the etymology: the name 'möglicherweise' (possibly) means 'Great of Rumbling'. Darnell and Darnell flag textual variants: the Seti I tomb and the sarcophagus of Tjaihorpata write 'he being sealed up' rather than 'from Re' (p. 199 n. 103); the word for 'lasso' is misplaced in all versions except Useramun (p. 200 n. 105); 'eye' could be read 'disk' (n. 104). Morenz's own caveats are unknown because the article was not read.
source_discrepancies: (1) Who enchants Apophis in Amduat Hour 7: the Royal Collection Trust page summary (search snippet only) and the Egypt Centre blog summary say 'Isis and Seth'; Darnell and Darnell (p. 11 n. 26) explicitly say the Elder Magician is 'not a hypostasis of Seth' but Heka. Older readings (e.g. Hornung) did equate the figure with Seth, which is the source of the popular version. Safe wording: Isis and the Elder Magician in the Amduat; Seth with his spear in other New Kingdom images and BD 108. (2) Length: Kockelmann gives 120 cubits as typical; Darnell and Darnell attribute the 120 cubits to Ptolemaic texts, while the New Kingdom Amduat gives 440 cubits for his sandbank (not his body). (3) Morenz 2004 dates the Ankhtifi attestation to the 9th Dynasty according to the Egypt Centre blog summary; Kockelmann says only First Intermediate Period. Not checked against Morenz. (4) Kockelmann says Apophis was not a deity, while Darnell and Darnell casually call Apep 'the god Apep' (p. 13). That is a wording difference, not a real disagreement: Darnell and Darnell show no cult either.
